A model has been outlined which predicts flow through cracks
under specified conditions (equations 5.7=5.9).

This model can be used to estimate the effective permeability
of chunam with cracks (Figures 5.12 and 5.13, equation 5.14).

From a field orack survey, chunam effective permeability was
predicted for poor to average chunam condition cover, as defined
by the CHASE report (Figure 5.14).

From the standpoint of geinfall intensity, an effective chunam
ermeability of 1 x 10 ms"' or less needs to be achieved
(Figure 5.15). This is the distinotion made in the summary
graph (Figure 5.14).

Selected factors have been outlined which may serve to reduce or
inorease the effective permeability of chunam for a specific
erack distribution. These are factors such as vertical crack
irregularity and void space at the chunam-soil interface that are
not modelled.

The effective permeability of 1 x 10-ma™1 renders the slope
independent of rainfall intensity (Figure 5.15), and in consequence,
only dependent on rainfall duration.

Whether 1 x 10~ma7! is a sufficiently low effective permeability
to render the underlying soil free from saturation under specific
rainfall duration recurrence intervals, can only be anawered by
reference to simulation studies undertaken by the soil water model
outlined in Section 3.0.
